title: Observability contract and emergency backstop for real-time LLM deployments
author: Sofia Ramirez
content:
Summary:
This guide defines the minimal telemetry contract and emergency backstop (safety fallback) that Customer Success and Integrations teams should negotiate and validate with enterprise customers before enabling real-time LLM routes (streaming generation, chat, or low-latency embedding lookups). It is intended for customers using Dedicated or Private deployments and for any Hosted customers with strict availability or regulatory constraints.

Why this matters:
- Real-time LLM workloads are bursty and dependent on model sizing, KV cache behavior, and GPU scheduling.
- Clear telemetry enables fast root cause identification and automated failover decisions without expensive manual triage.
- A pre-agreed backstop ensures customer-facing apps remain available while we remediate model-serving or network incidents.

When to use this guide:
1) Prior to go-live for any enterprise cutover that relies on streaming / sub-200ms tail latencies.
2) When onboarding customers with internal SLAs that require deterministic error-handling and audit trails.

Definitions and scope:
- Observability contract: a minimal list of events, metrics, and traces the customer must forward or allow Redwood to collect via the agreed telemetry connector.
- Emergency backstop: pre-approved fallthrough behavior (e.g., degraded model variant, cached response, throttled-preset response, or traffic diversion) executed automatically when thresholds are hit.
- Tenant: the customer-specific logical instance (dedicated or tenant on a shared runtime).
- SLO: service level objective for latency, availability, and quality.

Telemetry contract (mandatory fields):
Provide or enable forward of the following keys at 1–10s granularity for real-time routes. If the customer cannot forward, integrate the Redwood telemetry sidecar described in the onboarding checklist.
- request.id (string): unique per-request identifier (UUID v4 preferred).
- tenant.id (string): tenant identifier assigned by Redwood.
- route.name (string): API route or logical endpoint, e.g., /v1/generate/chat.
- model.name (string): canonical model id used for the request.
- model.variant (string): quantized or fallback variant if applicable.
- request.start_ts, request.end_ts (ISO 8601): timestamps.
- request.tokens.input (int), request.tokens.output (int): token counts.
- latency.p50, latency.p95, latency.p99 (ms): per-minute aggregations.
- error.code (string) and error.class (string): categorization (e.g., retryable, quota, capacity, network).
- kvcache.hit_rate (float 0..1): prefix cache hit rate (per-model or per-tenant).
- gpu.util_pct (float 0..100): per-host or per-cluster.
- queue.depth (int): pending requests queue length.
- fallback.invocations (int): count of automatic fallbacks triggered.

Optional enrichments (recommended):
- request.prompt_hash (string): deterministic hash for prompt family grouping.
- quality.eval_score (float): if customer sends sample eval scores for production prompts.
- upstream.region, upstream.zone (string): hosting region tags.

Representation examples (JSON telemetry envelope):
{
  "request.id": "b2d9f9a8-2c34-4f6c-8a2b-c3a9a5f0e41f",
  "tenant.id": "acme-corp-42",
  "route.name": "/v1/generate/chat",
  "model.name": "redwood-7b-quant",
  "request.start_ts": "2026-03-01T15:04:05Z",
  "request.end_ts": "2026-03-01T15:04:05.180Z",
  "latency.p95": "180",
  "error.class": "none"
}

SLOs and thresholds (example customer baseline):
- Availability: 99.9% (client-consumable successful responses per rolling 30d).
- Tail latency: p95 < 250ms for streaming-start; p99 < 1.2s.
- Failure budget burn: >5% sustained over 6 hours triggers escalation.

Automated detection rules (implement these prior to cutover):
1) Latency surge: p95 increases by 2x vs baseline for 5 consecutive 1-minute buckets -> alert to oncall, reduce accepted concurrency by 25% and start backstop handshake.
2) KV cache collapse: kvcache.hit_rate drops below 0.25 for 2 minutes -> throttle low-priority tenants first, begin passive warming and notify customer.
3) Queue depth grow: queue.depth > 500 for a tenant for 30s -> reject new streaming requests with HTTP 429 and return backstop token.
4) Quality regression: quality.eval_score drop > 0.1 for a set of production prompts -> pause auto-quantized rollouts and route to a higher-fidelity variant.

Emergency backstop options (ordered by preference):
A) Serve from warm KV cache snapshot (fastest, preserves freshest user context).
B) Switch to a pinned, higher-latency but more reliable variant in same region (e.g., redwood-13b -> redwood-7b-high-qa).
C) Return a degraded but deterministic response (pre-approved template) for low-risk routes (e.g., confirmation flows).
D) Reroute to a customer-managed model endpoint (for Private deployments with mirror endpoints).
E) Soft-throttle: reject with HTTP 429 + Retry-After header and a short JSON body explaining the backstop.

Backstop handshake protocol (6-step automated flow):
1) Detection: Redwood autoscalers or SLO monitor fires detection alert (rule above).
2) Pre-check: orchestration checks model compatibility and pre-warms target variant for 30s.
3) Soft switch: route 10% of traffic to backstop variant for 60s, compare latency and quality heuristics.
4) Validation: if soft switch metrics are acceptable for 60s, increase to 100% and mark fallthrough_active=true.
5) Notification: send immediate notification to customer via configured channel (webhook/email/snowflake). Include request samples and telemetry digest.
6) Recovery: when baseline metrics recover for 10 minutes, orchestrator gradually switches back and logs change.

Onboarding checklist (customer + Redwood pre-cutover):
- Customer: agree telemetry fields and retention window (minimum 7d), provide endpoint for webhook or enable sidecar.
- Customer: designate 1 primary and 1 secondary operator with contact info and oncall windows.
- Redwood: pre-provision pinned fallback variant and capacity reservations for first 72 hours of go-live.
- Redwood: deploy tenant-specific alert rules into customer’s alerting workspace or coordinate forwarding.
- Joint: run canary with synthetic journey at 50 RPS for 30 minutes and validate contract keys are arriving.
- Joint: run failure injection (latency + 5% error spike) to verify backstop activation and notification plumbing.

Escalation matrix (who to call when):
- Triage (0–15 min): Customer Ops oncall (customer-success) + Redwood Integration Engineer.
- Incident (15–90 min): Redwood SRE lead + Customer engineering escalation contact.
- Major outage (>90 min): Eng SRE Director, Customer VP Engineering, and Account Executive.
- Post-incident (24–72h): Joint RCA and action items tracked in QBR deck.

Operational runbook (step-by-step for oncall):
1) Acknowledge alert. Post initial note to incident channel with request.id examples and affected tenants.
2) Pull last 15 minutes of the telemetry contract keys (use the telemetry query snippet below).
3) If backstop is not active, trigger soft-switch via admin CLI and monitor p95/p99 for 5 minutes.
4) If soft-switch fails, escalate to SRE and enable HTTP 429 policy with sanitized messaging.
5) Collect 10 representative request payloads and forward to customer-ops for quality review.
6) Schedule a hot patch or rollback of recent rollout (model/quantization) if identified as root cause.

Telemetry query snippet (prometheus / clickhouse style pseudo-queries):
- p95 latency per tenant (PromQL):
  histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket{tenant=~"acme.*"}[1m])) by (le))
- kvcache hit rate (ClickHouse):
  SELECT tenant_id, sum(hit) / sum(hit + miss) as hit_rate FROM telemetry.kvcache WHERE event_ts > now() - interval 5 minute GROUP BY tenant_id

Example admin CLI (safe mode):
# soft-switch 10% traffic for tenant
redwood admin route-split --tenant acme-corp-42 --route /v1/generate/chat --weight 10 --variant redwood-7b-high-qa --dry-run

Customer messaging templates (to be used by CS during incident):
- Short status update: "We observed an elevated latency event impacting your streaming route. We have activated an automated backstop and are monitoring performance. No additional action required at this time. ETA for full restore: 30–90 minutes."
- Technical summary for engineers: include request IDs, telemetry digest, fallback.invocations and patch/rollback actions.

QBR metrics and post-incident items to include:
- Number of backstop activations (30/60/90 day).
- Mean time to backstop and mean time to recover.
- Top 5 prompt families causing highest cost during backstop windows.
- Action items tracked and closure dates.

Frequently observed edge cases and workarounds:
- Symptom: intermittent HTTP 502 with p95 stable but p99 spikes.
  Workaround: increase model.variant pool size, enable KV cache pre-warm, and temporarily reduce accepted concurrency.
- Symptom: customer cannot forward request.id (legacy proxy).
  Workaround: Redwood sidecar will inject a stamped request_id and mark origin=sidecar for traceability.
- Symptom: Private deployment with no outbound telemetry.
  Workaround: enable batched secure pull (SFTP or S3) with 30s max delay and use a separate compensating alert for delayed telemetry.

Ownership and SLAs:
- Customer Success: primary owner for communication and QBR follow-up.
- Integrations team: responsible for onboarding the telemetry connector and running the initial failure injection.
- Eng SRE: owns alert rules, backstop orchestration, and CLI tooling.
- SLAs are contractual; this document defines operational defaults but customer contracts may override thresholds.

Appendix A — Telemetry retention and privacy:
- Minimum retention for high-fidelity telemetry: 7d. Aggregated metrics must be stored for 90d for QBRs.
- PII: telemetry must not include customer PII. Use prompt_hash for grouping rather than raw prompt text unless explicitly consented and encrypted at rest.

Appendix B — Sample canary script (bash):
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# simple canary runner to exercise route and verify telemetry arrival
for i in {1..300}; do
  REQUEST_ID=$(uuidgen)
  curl -s -X POST https://api.redwood.example/v1/generate/chat \n    -H "Authorization: Bearer ${REDWOOD_KEY}" \n    -H "X-Request-ID: ${REQUEST_ID}" \n    -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello"}]}' >/dev/null &
  sleep 0.2
done
